attributes.description: Fires when a replication slot is retaining a large volume of WAL. An inactive slot pins WAL indefinitely and will eventually fill the data volume, which makes slot lag a disk-space risk rather than only a replication concern.
attributes.name: [Supabase OTel] Replication slot retaining WAL

investigation_guide.blob:
## Replication Slot Retaining WAL

PostgreSQL will not recycle WAL that a replication slot still needs. An abandoned slot — a replica that was removed, or a logical replication consumer that stopped reading — therefore accumulates WAL on the primary until the data volume is full. This is one of the least obvious ways to run out of disk.

### Triage Steps
1. Compare retained WAL against free space on the data mountpoint. Retention only matters relative to the volume it will fill: `TS metrics-supabase.metrics.otel-* | STATS avail = MIN(LAST_OVER_TIME(node_filesystem_avail_bytes)) BY attributes.mountpoint`
2. Establish whether the consumer is alive. A slot whose consumer is gone will never advance and must be dropped; a slow consumer will catch up if it is unblocked.
3. Check the WAL archive backlog (`pg_ls_archive_statusdir_wal_pending_count`) as a second, independent reason WAL may not be recycled.
4. Check `pg_wal_size_mb` growth to project when the volume will fill.

### Escalation
If retention is growing and free space is projected to run out, this becomes an imminent write outage. Treat it with the urgency of a disk-full alert rather than a replication alert.

### Tuning
The default is 10 GB of retained WAL. Size this against the free space on your data volume — on small compute tiers a much lower value is already dangerous. Slot series only exist when a replication slot exists, so projects without one return no rows.
